paragraphs.title: God’s Love and Care for Israel

easy.explanation: The verse says, “I called my son out of Egypt.”
easy.q: From which land did God call His son?

easy.explanation: The LORD says, “I taught Ephraim also to go, taking them by their arms.”
easy.q: Who taught Ephraim to go and took him by the arms?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “they knew not that I healed them.”
easy.q: What did God do for Israel even though Israel did not know it?

answers: With cords of a man and bands of love
medium.explanation: The KJV says, “I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love.”
medium.q: How did God draw Israel to Himself?

medium.explanation: God was like one who takes off “the yoke on their jaws.”
medium.q: What did God remove from Israel’s jaws?

medium.explanation: The verse says, “I laid meat unto them.”
medium.q: What did God lay before Israel?

answers: Calling Israel, teaching him, drawing him, and feeding him
Punishing Israel, exiling him, and forgetting him
Sending Israel to Assyria and withholding food
challenge.explanation: The passage presents God’s continuing care through calling, teaching, loving, freeing, and feeding Israel.
challenge.q: What progression of care is described in these verses?

answers: God cared for Israel, but Israel did not recognize it
God rejected Israel, but Israel understood everything
God ignored Israel, but Israel praised Him
challenge.explanation: Although God healed and cared for Israel, “they knew not” that He had done so.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between God’s actions and Israel’s understanding?

answers: He relieved and cared for him
challenge.explanation: Removing the yoke portrays God as easing Israel’s burden and providing for him.
challenge.q: What does the image of removing the yoke suggest about God’s treatment of Israel?

paragraphs.title: Israel’s Turning Away and Its Consequences

easy.explanation: The verse says, “the Assyrian shall be his king.”
easy.q: Which kingdom would be Israel’s king instead of Egypt?

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “the sword shall abide on his cities.”
easy.q: What would abide on Israel’s cities?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “my people are bent to backsliding from me.”
easy.q: How are God’s people described in verse 7?

medium.explanation: The verse gives the reason: “because they refused to return.”
medium.q: Why would the Assyrian be Israel’s king?

medium.explanation: The sword would “consume his branches, and devour them.”
The verse says the sword would devour them “because of their own counsels.”
medium.q: What caused the destruction described in verse 6?

answers: They were called to the most High, but would not exalt Him
They were called to war, but won a victory
They were called to Egypt, but returned to Jerusalem
challenge.explanation: Though they were called to the most High, “none at all would exalt him.”
challenge.q: What is the main contrast in the people’s behavior in verse 7?

answers: Because they refused to return, Assyria became their king
Because they returned, Assyria protected them
Because they trusted God, Assyria left them
challenge.explanation: Their refusal to return is directly given as the reason Assyria would rule them.
challenge.q: How does the passage connect Israel’s refusal to return with Assyria?

answers: A people refusing to return, relying on wrong counsels, and facing destruction
A people trusting God and receiving peace
A people leaving Assyria and settling safely in Egypt
challenge.explanation: The verses describe refusal, backsliding, reliance on their own counsels, and the sword upon their cities.
challenge.q: What overall picture is presented in verses 5–7?

easy.explanation: God asks, “How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?” and says His heart is turned within Him.
easy.q: For whom does God’s heart turn within Him?

easy.explanation: God says, “I will not return to destroy Ephraim.”
easy.q: What does God say He will not do to Ephraim?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “for I am God, and not man.”
easy.q: Why does God not act like a man?

medium.explanation: The phrase describes God’s compassion and inward mercy toward Ephraim.
medium.q: What does “my repentings are kindled together” express in context?

medium.explanation: God’s heart is turned and His repentings are kindled, so He does not destroy Ephraim.
medium.q: What keeps God from carrying out the fierceness of His anger?

medium.explanation: God mentions the fierceness of His anger but chooses not to destroy Ephraim.
medium.q: What contrast appears in these verses?

answers: His compassion makes Him unwilling to abandon Ephraim
He has decided to deliver Ephraim to Assyria
challenge.explanation: The questions show God’s deep reluctance to give up or destroy His people.
challenge.q: What does God’s question, “How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?” reveal?

answers: He is God, not man, and the Holy One is in the midst of Israel
He is the king of Assyria
He is far away from Israel
challenge.explanation: God explains His mercy by saying, “I am God, and not man; the Holy One in the midst of thee.”
challenge.q: How does verse 9 explain the uniqueness of God’s response?

answers: Judgment is deserved, but God chooses not to destroy Ephraim
Israel is innocent, but God destroys him
God wants to restore Israel, but Israel is already home
challenge.explanation: The passage holds together the seriousness of judgment and God’s merciful decision not to destroy.
challenge.q: What is the central tension in verses 8–9?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “They shall walk after the LORD.”
The verse says, “he shall roar like a lion.”
easy.q: Like what animal will the LORD roar?

easy.explanation: God promises, “I will place them in their houses.”
easy.q: What will God do with the returning people?

medium.explanation: The verse says, “when he shall roar, then the children shall tremble.”
medium.q: What happens when the LORD roars?

medium.explanation: They will come “as a bird out of Egypt” and “as a dove out of the land of Assyria.”
medium.q: From which two places will the people return?

answers: His call causes them to follow and come back
His roar prevents them from returning
His roar brings the sword upon them
medium.explanation: After the LORD roars, the children tremble and return from distant lands.
medium.q: What is the relationship between the LORD’s roar and the people’s return?

challenge.explanation: The trembling birds suggest a fearful and urgent return.
challenge.q: What do the bird and dove images suggest about the returning people?

answers: The LORD roars, the people tremble, they return, and they are placed in their houses
The sword falls, the people are exiled, and their houses are destroyed
The people worship idols, leave Egypt, and conquer Assyria
challenge.explanation: The passage gives this sequence: God’s roar, the people’s trembling, their return, and their restoration to their houses.
challenge.q: What sequence is presented in verses 10–11?

answers: From scattering and distance to returning and dwelling in their houses
From homes to permanent exile in Assyria
From following God to worshiping idols
challenge.explanation: The people come from distant lands and are placed again in their houses.
challenge.q: What is the main change in Israel’s condition at the end of the passage?
